newsitem.title: USA: Global telecom deal opens new markets to U.S firms.
newsitem.headline: Global telecom deal opens new markets to U.S firms.

text.p: U.S. Trade Representative Designate Charlene Barshefsky said on Saturday that a landmark global telecommunications trade agreement will open new markets for U.S. firms and lower costs to consumers.

Barshefsky told a news conference that the agreement reached in Geneva on Saturday after months of difficult negotiations will unleash competition in markets representing more than 95 percent of global telecommunications revenues.
"A 60-year tradition of telecommunications monopolies and closed markets has been replaced by market opening, deregulation and competition," Barshefsky said.
"Before this agreement, only 17 percent of the top 20 telecom markets were open to U.S. companies; now they have access to nearly 100 percent of these markets," she added.
Barshefsky said the deal could double or triple the size of the $600 billion telecommunications industry in 10 years.
President Bill Clinton said the United States would reap significant economic benefits from the accord negotiated under the auspices of the World Trade Organization (WTO).

"Today's agreement will bring clear benefits to American workers, businesses and consumers alike -- new jobs, new markets and lower prices -- and will spread the benefits of a technology revolution to citizens around the world," the president said in a statement.

A long list of U.S. companies praised the deal and a number of representatives of major firms, including AT&T, MCI and Sprint joined Barshefsky and Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt at Saturday's news conference.
Barshefsky said the agreement should lower the costs of international telephone calls from an average $1 per minute to 20 cents per minute over the next several years.

"The world's businesses today spend more money on telecommunications than on oil," Barshefsky said. "Less expensive and better telecom services means that the United States and other nations that are active in global trade will reduce one of their largest costs of doing business."

The deal struck on Saturday was far better than what was offered last April when the United States walked away from the talks. Barshefsky said at that time only 47 countries had made offers and that they covered only about 60 percent of global telecommunications revenues, of which half represented the U.S. market.
The agreement will open the U.S. market up to more foreign competition as well. Foreign firms will be able to acquire up to 100 percent of U.S. companies through U.S. subsidiaries, Barshefsky said.

But two important U.S. trading partners, Japan and Canada, did not open up to full foreign ownership. Barshefsky said she was disappointed Canada retained a 46.7 percent limit on foreign ownership and that Japan maintained limits on foreign investment in its existing telecommunications companies.
"Japan keeping those restrictions sends a terrible signal to many countries around the world who hide behind Japan's restrictions as justification for their own," Barshefsky said.

In response to Canada's refusal to raise its investment limits, the United States retained some restrictions on foreign ownership of U.S.-based direct-to-home and broadcast satellite services, Barshefsky said.

Barshefsky said she plans to work with Congress on laws to implement the trade agreement. U.S. trade officials had said they felt they had sufficient authority under existing law to implement the deal, which is to take effect in December. But some lawmakers had questioned whether Barshefsky had legal authority to implement the deal without legislation.

"Any trade agreement of this magnitude needs to be examined and scrutinized before one can fully assess the implications for both telecommunications and U.S. trade policy," Representative Ed Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat, said in a statement.
